newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania airport reopens, capital returns to normal.
newsitem.headline: Albania airport reopens, capital returns to normal.

text.p: Tirana airport reopened for business on Thursday, the most visible sign so far that Albania's capital is returning to normal after days of unrest, although it could be some days before scheduled flights resume.

The chief of police at Rinas airport, 25 km (16 miles) west of Tirana, told Reuters the facility had been secured by special forces, all key staff were in place and it was ready to operate at any moment.

Western airlines say they do not plan to resume regular flights to and from Tirana until Sunday at the earliest. However the Bulgarian embassy said it planned to fly out a group of its own and other nationals later on Thursday.

The airport is Albania's main gateway to the outside world, and staging point for any flow of humanitarian aid that its government and European observers say it will require soon to cope with food and other shortages.

Some 40 km (25 miles) west of the capital the Italian navy on Thursday completed a dramatic rescue operation to save an Albanian fishing boat packed with 350 refugees that had risked sinking in stormy seas off the Albanian coast, an Italian spokesman said.
The rescue, lasting nearly 24 hours, took place in strong winds that had blown the ship to within 14 miles of the Albanian coast.
The Italian frigate Espero towed the boat to a calmer bay north of the Albanian port of Durres.
The refugees, who included 45 children, were then taken by landing craft to a beach in the Bay of Rodon, from where they were to be taken by bus to Tirana and other destinations.
Navy officials denied Italian media reports that marines had landed in Albania to begin a humanitarian operation.

The reopening of Tirana airport, foreshadowed in a government announcement on Tuesday, was a further indication the capital was returning to normal after days of near-anarchy last week sparked by looting of weapons from army depots.
However unrest was reported from some other parts of the country, mainly in the south which is mostly under the control of rebels demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha.
In the town of Korce, some 180 km (110 miles) south-east of Tirana, residents reached by telephone reported that gunmen had looted all the town's shops and that shooting was continuing.
Two days ago the town's mediaeval museum, the only one in the country, was also looted.
An Austrian television crew said gunmen stole all their luggage and equipment in Pogradec, on the shores of Lake Ohrid, on the road to Korce on Wednesday.
In the south rebel leaders were still awaiting a visit by Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, who heads an all-party government called to restore order and organise elections by June.

Fino had been expected in the rebel town of Gjirokaster on Wednesday. A spokesman for the premier in Tirana told Reuters, however, that Fino had too much to do in the capital and would not even be travelling on Thursday.

An umbrella group of rebel leaders in the south had called on Berisha to quit by Thursday, with an implied threat of military action if he refused. However a rebel leader indicated on Wednesday they would not use force.
Government leaders said calls for Berisha's resignation were a threat to the country's fragile institutions.

"If President Berisha gives in to such a request...a constitutional vacuum would be created in Albania," Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova told a news conference in Rome on Wednesday. "That's not good for the country."
The rebels accuse Berisha of allowing shady pyramid savings schemes to flourish, and of failing to warn people of the risks. Thousands lost their life savings in the schemes.

Berisha has pledged to step down if his Democratic Party, elected in 1992 and re-elected by a landslide in May 1996 polls branded seriously flawed by international observers, loses the new elections this summer.
